source.title: DSPA: Dynamic SAE Steering for Data-Efficient Preference Alignment
source.authors: J. Wedgwood; Aashiq Muhamed; Mona T. Diab; Virginia Smith

record.file_problem: No garbling or cutoff is apparent. Some ablation results are shown only in figures and lack transcribed numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: The study audits SAE feature sets and reports that feature interpretations can differ between base and fine-tuned SAEs, qualifying the idea that SAE features are stable, canonical units. It does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper uses SAE features to steer preference behavior but does not measure feature overlap or superposition in the toy-model sense, polysemanticity, or SAE recovery of model features. Main benchmark results concern preference alignment, not the claim versions. The cited superposition account is background, not a result of this study. The paper's feature-set comparison and interpretation mismatch are the results relevant to V5.
record.test_reason: DSPA is a preference-alignment steering method that uses SAEs as a tool. Its results are benchmark scores for its own method plus an audit of the features it edits. The base-vs-fine-tuned SAE comparison (App. B.2) counts overlap between the method's own candidate steering sets and gives one anecdotal LLM-labelled interpretation change. It does not measure whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units of the model, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is incomplete. The authors' main conclusion is that DSPA, a prompt-conditional inference-time SAE steering method, improves MT-Bench on Gemma-2-2B/9B and Qwen3-8B, and is competitive on AlpacaEval except on Gemma-2-9B. It also preserves multiple-choice accuracy and is data-efficient (robust at N=250, and down to 100 on Gemma-2-2B). Their audit finds preference directions dominated by discourse and stylistic features, with feature labels that are approximate and LLM-generated. The base-vs-fine-tuned SAE analysis is a side appendix used to justify sparsifying A, not a stated conclusion about feature stability.
record.recipe_differences: No reproduction of the original toy-model superposition method; this paper studies inference-time SAE steering for preference alignment in LLMs.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE choice (base versus HH-RLHF fine-tuned) changes candidate feature-set sizes and at least one reported feature interpretation.

fits_no_version.finding: After fine-tuning a Gemma Scope SAE on HH-RLHF, feature index 10776 gets a different LLM-generated interpretation: harmful activities (fine-tuned) vs. hedging language (base). The method's candidate steering sets overlap partially (40/76 augment, 49/83 ablate).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE feature identities at fixed indices can drift when the SAE is fine-tuned on domain data (anecdotal, LLM-labelled).

record.problems: The relevant feature interpretations are LLM-generated and not systematically human-validated. The base-versus-fine-tuned comparison is limited to Gemma-2-9B, and the reported index-set intersections do not establish semantic identity or completeness. Some ablation results are figure-only.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were left out as claim-relevant rows. The feature-category counts and benchmark outcomes do not test the listed superposition or SAE-canonicality claims.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: no capacity or polysemanticity analysis.
The study uses SAEs but does not evaluate whether they recover the model's sparse features or measure how features are distributed across neurons.
No systematic test of completeness, stability across seeds or SAE methods, or canonicality. The base-vs-fine-tuned comparison concerns the method's selected sets plus one anecdote.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition is cited only as background (Elhage et al. 2022). The reader's T5 'challenges V5' label overreads an appendix anecdote and selection-set overlaps. The fine-tuned-vs-base SAE steering performance difference (Fig. 5B) is method performance, not a claim test.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model feature overlap, geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
Whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or whether SAEs recover sparse model features; the study uses SAEs but does not evaluate those claims.

Tests a limited comparison of selected feature sets and one reported interpretation mismatch between base and fine-tuned SAEs for Gemma-2-9B. Does not establish completeness, causal validity, or canonicality across models, layers, seeds, or SAE methods.
Whether the model's represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Compared base and fine-tuned SAE candidate augment-feature index sets, using the top 16 indices per input feature.

conditions.value: base Gemma Scope and HH-RLHF fine-tuned

rows.measure: Number of shared feature indices between candidate augment sets
rows.note: The sets share some indices, but their sizes differ and the reported intersection is not the full set of either version.
rows.check: This is a selection value: overlap of DSPA's top-16 augment candidate sets derived from the conditional-difference map A. Set size and overlap reflect the method's selection, not whether SAE features are stable units. The 'baseline' is set sizes, not a control.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Compared base and fine-tuned SAE candidate ablate-feature index sets, using the top 16 indices per input feature.

conditions.value: base Gemma Scope and HH-RLHF fine-tuned

rows.measure: Number of shared feature indices between candidate ablate sets
rows.note: The sets share some indices, but their sizes differ and the reported intersection is not the full set of either version.
rows.check: Same issue as r1, for the ablate candidate sets (base 186, fine-tuned 83, 49 shared). The authors read this as concentration of the preference map, not as feature stability.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9B
rows.operation_detail: Compared generated interpretations for feature index 10776 across base and fine-tuned SAEs.

conditions.value: base Gemma Scope and HH-RLHF fine-tuned

rows.measure: Agreement of the feature's generated interpretation across SAE versions
rows.baseline: Fine-tuned SAE: questions or statements involving illegal or clearly harmful activities
rows.value: Base SAE: hedging or clarification language expressing uncertainty or confusion
rows.note: The paper reports that interpretations do not always match; these interpretations were generated by an LLM and were not systematically validated by humans.
rows.check: A single anecdote: feature 10776 gets different gpt-5-mini labels in the base SAE and in an SAE fine-tuned from it on HH-RLHF. The labels are not human-validated, and there is no systematic stability measure or rate. Index correspondence after deliberate fine-tuning is not the stability or canonicality V5 names.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Gemma-2-9B candidate feature sets and feature interpretation compared between base Gemma Scope and HH-RLHF fine-tuned SAEs
reader_labels.reason: The candidate sets have limited reported overlap, and feature 10776 receives different interpretations across SAE versions, challenging stable canonical interpretation in this tested comparison (r1-r3).
